justification:
Confirmed on the worktree (branch issue-55-http-explained) before starting; made no commits.

All four round-1 findings verified fixed against primary sources, independently re-fetched rather than trusted from the writer's description:

1) Major -- ETag/RFC 9110 8.8.3 misattribution. Fetched RFC 9110 section 8.8.3 by curling the plaintext RFC and grepping to the exact line range (the summarizing WebFetch tool truncated the HTML edition before section 8 and, on one plaintext attempt, produced a hallucinated RFC-7231-era sentence that does not exist in RFC 9110 at all -- I do not trust that path for this claim and instead read the raw section 8.8.3 text myself at rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.txt lines 3570-3610). The actual text: 'An entity tag is an opaque validator for differentiating between multiple representations of the same resource...'. The article's quote -- '"an opaque validator for differentiating between multiple representations of the same resource"' cited to RFC 9110 section 8.8.3 -- is now genuinely verbatim and correctly attributed. Separately, I fetched RFC 9111 section 4.3.1 (rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9111.txt lines 812-843) and confirmed it reads verbatim: 'One or more entity tags, indicating one or more stored responses, can be used in an If-None-Match header field for response validation, or in an If-Match or If-Range header field for representation selection.' This sits in the subsection 'Sending a Validation Request,' which is explicitly about a cache synthesizing a conditional request from a stored response's entity tag -- exactly the context the article now uses it in ('A client that still has a stored response sends that token back in If-None-Match -- RFC 9111 describes exactly this: ...'). Both quotes are now correctly sourced and correctly contextualized; the misattribution is fully resolved.

2) Minor -- safe-implies-idempotent citation. Fetched RFC 9110 section 9.2.2 via the same raw-text method (lines 3861-3873) and confirmed it reads verbatim: 'A request method is considered "idempotent" if the intended effect on the server of multiple identical requests with that method is the same as the effect for a single such request. Of the request methods defined by this specification, PUT, DELETE, and safe request methods are idempotent.' The article's claim ('Safe methods... are idempotent by construction') is now cited to 9.2.2, which is exactly the section that states this. The citation was moved consistently everywhere else in the article that references idempotency (four total occurrences, all now pointing to 9.2.2 correctly).

3) Moderate -- TcpListener.Start citation. Fetched the real TcpListener.Start Microsoft Learn page. Its Remarks section reads verbatim: 'The Start method initializes the underlying Socket, binds it to a local endpoint, and listens for incoming connection attempts. If a connection request is received, the Start method will queue the request and continue listening for additional requests until you call the Stop method.' The article's new quote -- 'initializes the underlying Socket, binds it to a local endpoint, and listens for incoming connection attempts,' queuing any connection request that arrives 'until you call the Stop method' -- is genuinely verbatim from the real page, and both the inline citation and the front-matter source entry now point at .../tcplistener.start instead of .../tcplistener.accepttcpclientasync. Confirmed no other in-body citation still points at the wrong AcceptTcpClientAsync page; the remaining AcceptTcpClientAsync mentions are all plain code/prose references to the method call itself, not citations.

4) Minor -- HOL-blocking citation. Fetched RFC 9112 section 9.3.2 (rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9112.txt lines 1397-1404), confirmed verbatim: 'A server MAY process a sequence of pipelined requests in parallel if they all have safe methods..., but it MUST send the corresponding responses in the same order that the requests were received.' The article's HTTP/1.1 bullet now cites section 9.3.2 specifically (not the parent 9.3) and quotes this exact MUST clause.

5) Minor -- ETag truncation caveat. The added note ('Why the tag is only 8 hex characters') states the demo keeps the first 8 hex characters (32 bits) of the SHA-256 digest, that this is fine for the demo's three requests but would collide too often in production, and that a real implementation should send the full 64-character/256-bit digest. This is accurate: `Convert.ToHexString(SHA256.HashData(...))[..8]` takes exactly 8 of 64 hex characters (4 of 32 bytes = 32 of 256 bits), and RFC 9110 8.8.1 (checked in round 1) only requires the tag be treated as an opaque string, so truncation doesn't violate the spec, only weakens collision resistance -- exactly what the note says.
